title: Many concurrent streams over ONE multiplexed connection

cases.purpose: N=32 threads share one connection; every result belongs to the statement that asked for it (no cross-stream delivery).
steps: One SDK connection (multiplexed). CREATE TABLE conf_c1 (id int8 PRIMARY KEY, v text); insert ids 1..1000 with v = 'row-' || id.
32 threads x 200 iterations: each picks a random id and runs SELECT id, v FROM conf_c1 WHERE id = $1 (half prepared, half literal SQL) on the SAME connection.
Check SHOW pdb.wire_protocol on that connection afterwards.
cases.expected: 6400 results, each exactly [id, 'row-'||id] for the id it asked; zero errors; protocol 'pdb-native-v2'.

cases.purpose: No head-of-line blocking: a slow statement does not delay fast ones on the same connection.
steps: One connection. Thread 1 runs SELECT pg_sleep(2).
100 ms later threads 2..9 each run SELECT 1 twenty times on the SAME connection.
cases.expected: All 160 fast statements finish before the slow one returns (each fast statement < 1 s).

cases.purpose: Two large result sets streamed concurrently on one connection both arrive complete and in order.
steps: One connection, two threads: SELECT g FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g and SELECT -g FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g, each iterated fully.
cases.expected: Each thread sees exactly its 200000 values in order (sum 20000100000 and -20000100000).

cases.purpose: Interleaved transactions on two connections are isolated; concurrent statements inside ONE connection's open transaction all see that transaction's writes.
steps: Connections A and B. CREATE TABLE conf_c4 (id int8 PRIMARY KEY, owner text).
A: BEGIN; INSERT (1,'a'). B: BEGIN; INSERT (2,'b').
On A, 8 threads concurrently SELECT owner FROM conf_c4 ORDER BY id (shared session, in A's transaction). On B likewise.
Commit both; read from a third connection.
cases.expected: A's threads all see only ['a']; B's only ['b']; afterwards ['a','b'].

cases.purpose: More concurrent statements than the server's advertised stream cap queue at the client instead of failing.
steps: One connection; disable any optional client-side rejection cap so this case isolates the server-advertised cap. Start (server stream cap x 3) threads, each running SELECT pg_sleep(0.05), 1 once.
cases.expected: Every statement returns 1; none fails with a stream-limit error.
